title: Visible and invisible (CCC 325–327)
hook: heaven and earth, angels and all that is

segments.voice: Yesterday, providence: God guiding a creation still on its way. Your line was we are co-workers. Today, everything that is, seen and unseen.

Take stock of the last minute. Air you can't see went in and out of your lungs. A signal nobody can see probably carried these words to wherever you are. Somewhere, someone's trust in you, which you can't see either, is part of why your day holds together. A lot of what holds a life up is invisible. The Creed said at Sunday Mass calls God the maker of all things visible and invisible. Today we stay with that phrase.
screen: `AIR YOU CAN'T SEE.` → `TRUST YOU CAN'T SEE.` → `ALL THINGS VISIBLE AND INVISIBLE.`

segments.voice: Start with the bigger phrase, heaven and earth. In scripture, the Catechism says, it means all that exists: creation as a whole. The earth is the world of people. Heaven can mean the sky, or God's own place, our Father who art in heaven, or the place of the angels around God. Then the Creed adds: visible and invisible. Paul says it in Colossians, in the Douay-Rheims: "in him were all things created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible." A Church council, quoted in the Catechism, put it plainly: from the beginning God made both orders of creation, the spiritual and the bodily, the angelic and the earthly, and then the human, made of both together. In the Catholic picture, people stand where the two orders meet: a body, like everything on earth, and a spirit. That's tomorrow, body and soul. Invisible here doesn't mean imaginary. It means real things eyes can't catch, like the angels and the human soul. The Creed holds that all of creation, seen and unseen, is made by God, and nothing created sits outside that making. Look back over this week: the faith handed down, scripture at four depths, I believe inside we believe, the Creed's three movements, power as mercy, providence and its co-workers, and now the maker of all things. In the Creed's one short phrase, the seen and the unseen stand side by side, on the same list of things made.
screen: `HEAVEN AND EARTH: ALL THAT EXISTS.` · `VISIBLE AND INVISIBLE, IN COLOSSIANS.` · `TWO ORDERS, AND HUMANS MADE OF BOTH.` · `INVISIBLE DOESN'T MEAN IMAGINARY.`

segments.voice: Feel the air coming in, cool, then going out, warm; you've never seen it. Now name one more invisible thing your life leans on, someone's loyalty, a promise kept, your own memory, a love you've been given, and let it be as real as the chair under you. If you pray, thank God, maker of things seen and unseen, for it; if you don't, simply let your attention rest there.
Visible and invisible. All that exists, seen and unseen, which the Creed says God made, from the angels to the air. Today's word.
Your line: seen and unseen. From the angels to the air, all on one list. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Sunday Mass Catholics profess God as maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible, and the Church keeps feasts for the angels in its calendar.

chat.says: If angels are invisible, are they just pretend, like imaginary friends?
options: In the Creed, invisible doesn't mean imaginary: it means real things eyes can't catch, all made by God.
Angels aren't made at all: the Creed says only the things we can see were created by God.
The Creed calls angels invisible because they live only in heaven and never touch the world.
chat.meaning: The Creed calls God maker of all things visible and invisible. Invisible means real but unseen, like angels and the soul, not imaginary.

Colossians.meaning: Paul's letter to the church at Colossae

Creed.meaning: the Church's statement of faith, said at Mass

orders of creation.meaning: the two kinds of things made: spiritual and bodily

notes: Catechism paraphrased (copyright): heaven and earth as all that exists; earth the world of men; heaven as firmament, God's 'place', and the place of the angels (CCC 326); the council (Lateran IV, quoted in CCC 327) on both orders of creation and the human made of both. The council is not named or dated in the voice, under the claims rule.
'our Father who art in heaven' is said without quotation marks as a familiar phrase; source listed as Matthew 6:9, paraphrased.
'All things visible and invisible' given as the Creed's phrase at Sunday Mass (Nicene Creed); not placed in quotation marks.
